1.title: Third-Party Risk and Compliance
1.text: Welcome to Module nineteen: Third-Party Risk and Compliance. It covers the exam area Security Program Management and Oversight. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. five point three Explain the assessment and management processes associated with third-party risk. five point four Summarize elements of effective security compliance. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Program Management and Oversight (fourteen percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Why third parties matter
1.text: Why third parties matter. Vendors, partners and cloud providers touch your data and systems, so their weaknesses become your risk (supply chain risk, module five). Third-party risk management covers choosing, contracting, monitoring and ending the relationship.

1.title: Why third parties matter, continued
1.text: Why third parties matter. The figure shows this: The vendor life cycle: select, contract, monitor, review, offboard.

1.title: Vendor selection
1.text: Vendor selection. Request for information (R F I). Gather general information about what vendors offer. Request for proposal (R F P). Detailed proposal with solution and price for a defined need. Request for quote (R F Q). Price for a well-defined product or service. Expression of interest (E O I). A vendor signals interest before the formal process. Due diligence. Investigating the vendor's security, finances and reputation before signing. Conflict of interest. A relationship that could bias the selection.

1.title: Agreement types
1.text: Agreement types. S L A (service level agreement) (service-level agreement). Measurable service levels and penalties (uptime, response time). S L O (service-level objective). A target inside an S L A. M O U (memorandum of understanding). Non-binding statement of shared intent. M O A (memorandum of agreement). Binding agreement on roles and actions. N D A (non-disclosure agreement). Keeps information confidential. M S A (master services agreement). Overall terms for a long-term relationship. S O W (statement of work). Specific tasks, deliverables and timeline of one project. Exam tip: M S A equals umbrella terms; S O W equals one project. S L A equals measurable service promise. M O U equals non-binding; M O A equals binding. N D A equals secrecy.

1.title: Vendor monitoring and limits
1.text: Vendor monitoring and limits. Right to audit. Contract clause letting you inspect the vendor. Service-level monitoring. Tracking performance against the S L A. Vendor registry. A list of vendors with their risk ratings. Vendor assessment. Questionnaires and reviews of vendor controls. Compliance attestation. A vendor's statement (often an independent report) that it meets a standard. Penetration testing. Testing the vendor's systems (with permission). Rules of engagement. Written limits and permissions for a test. Limitations and constraints: staffing, resource availability, environment, legal and regulatory factors, geography and jurisdiction, financial or R O I limits, vendor lock-in, assurance mechanisms.

1.title: Security compliance
1.text: Security compliance. Compliance training. Data handling, anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing (A M L or C T F), anti-bribery. Compliance monitoring. Attestations (formal statements) and acknowledgements (people confirm they read policies). Consequences of non-compliance. Reputational damage, financial, legal, contractual, sanctions, loss of license. Privacy. Right to be forgotten, opt-in or opt-out, data correction, processing restrictions, processing prevention, controller versus processor, ownership. Legal compliance. Legal hold (preserve data for litigation), legal orders, data retention requirements. Exam tip: A legal hold stops normal deletion of relevant data; retention requirements set how long data must be kept.

1.title: Security compliance, continued
1.text: Security compliance. The figure shows this: Privacy rights: erasure, correction, restriction, consent, with controller and processor roles. Exam tip: A legal hold overrides normal deletion: nothing relevant may be destroyed. A controller decides the purpose; a processor handles data on its behalf. Right to be forgotten equals erasure on request, subject to law.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors already has a long-term contract with a supplier and now wants a document that defines one new project's tasks and deliverables. Which should it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A statement of work. A statement of work defines the specific tasks and deliverables, under the umbrella of the M S A.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A contract lets the company inspect a cloud provider's security controls on request. Which clause is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Right to audit. A right to audit clause allows inspection of the vendor's controls.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company wants vendors to describe their offerings in general before it defines requirements. Which document fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: R F I. A request for information gathers general information from vendors.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Litigation is expected, so all emails about the project must be preserved even though the policy says to delete them after ninety days. What applies? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Legal hold. A legal hold suspends normal deletion for relevant data.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A customer asks a company to delete the personal data it holds about them. Which privacy right is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Right to be forgotten. Requesting erasure of personal data is the right to be forgotten.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. An agreement states uptime of ninety-nine point nine percent and credits if the vendor misses it. Which agreement is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: S L A. A service-level agreement sets measurable service levels and remedies.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between R F I, R F P and R F Q? Answer: R F I gathers information, R F P asks for a detailed proposal, R F Q asks for a price. Question two. What does an M S A cover? Answer: The overall terms of a long-term vendor relationship. Question three. What is due diligence? Answer: Investigating a vendor's security, finances and reputation before signing.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name three consequences of non-compliance. Answer: For example reputational damage, financial penalties, legal action, sanctions, loss of license. Question five. What is a compliance attestation? Answer: A formal statement, often independent, that a standard is met. Question six. Controller or processor: who decides why data is processed? Answer: The controller.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Selection: R F I (information), R F P (proposal), R F Q (price), E O I; due diligence; conflict of interest. Agreements: S L A or S L O, M O U (non-binding), M O A (binding), N D A, M S A (umbrella), S O W (project). Monitoring: right to audit, service-level monitoring, vendor registry and assessments, attestations, penetration testing, rules of engagement. Compliance: training (data handling, A M L or C T F, anti-bribery), attestations and acknowledgements, consequences, privacy rights, legal hold and retention. In the next module, we continue the course.
